HR@10 against 99 sampled negatives measures ranking within a 100-item candidate set. It does not establish full-catalog HR@10 improvement. Krichene and Rendle show sampled metrics can reverse model comparisons even in expectation; repeating negative sampling cannot eliminate this systematic bias. Keep the pinned evaluator unchanged and describe gains specifically as sampled-candidate validation improvements. [On Sampled Metrics](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/)

For this benchmark, a practical uncertainty diagnostic is a paired bootstrap: resample users within each category, preserve each user’s baseline–candidate pairing and fixed candidates, then recompute the equally weighted four-category mean difference. Report the difference, its interval and category-level changes. With 200 users/category, one additional hit changes category HR@10 by 0.005 and the macro average by 0.00125. These intervals describe user-sampling uncertainty conditional on the trained models and candidate sets; they exclude training-seed and candidate-sampling variability. User-level paired comparisons are supported by [Assessing ranking metrics](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10791-020-09377-x).

Repeatedly selecting the best checkpoint or configuration on the same validation users introduces selection optimism. A bootstrap interval computed after selection does not automatically account for that adaptive search. Treat small winning differences as provisional, record the selection process, and reserve generalization claims for the host’s final held-out evaluation under its stated protocol. Neither validation gains nor narrow intervals establish full-catalog improvement. [Cawley and Talbot](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v11/cawley10a.html) document how optimizing noisy selection criteria can overfit model selection.
